title: lorastats v1

data.$comment: A CLOSED enumeration of the three dialects production sends (ZC answered 4 Sep 2026: 'make it work for all the known dialects'). oneOf rather than anyOf on purpose: the three branches are disjoint by field name and value type, so a record matching two of them is a modelling error and oneOf surfaces it as a validation failure instead of silently picking the first match. A FOURTH spelling matches no branch and dead-letters at the Writer, because a union allowed to grow silently is a contract nobody understands. Detection in Java is STRUCTURAL and mirrors these branches; `version` is 1 on all three and discriminates nothing.

counterInteger.$comment: Unbounded here on purpose. The signed BIGINT ceiling is enforced by the Writer before conversion, because JSON Schema's `maximum` on an integer this wide is evaluated as a double by some validators and would silently admit a value it cannot represent.

counterString.$comment: Dialect B sends every counter as a string. Constrained to digits only and capped at 19 digits, exactly as the netstats counters are: a non-numeric value dead-letters at the Writer rather than failing a cast at query time. The gap between this 19-digit ceiling and the signed BIGINT maximum 9223372036854775807 is not expressible as a regex, so the Writer MUST range-check before conversion - an unchecked overflow corrupts the value with no error.

dialectBareInteger.title: dialect A - bare names, integer values
dialectBareInteger.$comment: The dialect encoded first, because it matches omsstats, which shares the same converter family. additionalProperties stays true: a member Heimdal adds between releases is VALID and is preserved in data_extra, never dropped.

dialectBareString.title: dialect B - bare names, STRING values
dialectBareString.$comment: timespan is typed as a STRING here even though no production dialect-B record carries it - the observed record omits it entirely. A dialect is internally consistent by definition, so a record mixing string counters with an integer timespan is not dialect B with one odd field; it is a shape nobody has explained, and the closed enumeration sends those to the DLQ where a human sees them rather than absorbing them. If such a record ever appears, that DLQ entry is the trigger to widen this branch deliberately.

dialectPrefixedInteger.title: dialect C - lora_-prefixed counters, integer values
dialectPrefixedInteger.$comment: THIS DIALECT IS NOT 'everything prefixed', and writing the branch from that description rejects the real traffic it was written to accept. The production record of 29 Aug 2026 (valid/lorastats-dialect-prefixed.json) carries fifteen lora_-prefixed counters alongside a BARE fsk_received and a BARE timespan. Both spellings of the two optional counters are typed here so the observed record and its plausible variants both validate; the REQUIRED set stays prefixed-only, which is what keeps the branch disjoint from dialects A and B and the enumeration closed.

$comment: THREE DIALECTS, ONE STORED SHAPE. Production lorastats arrives in three mutually incompatible payload dialects - bare/integer, bare/string ('176'), and lora_-prefixed/integer - and all three carry version:1, so nothing on the record discriminates them. ZC answered on 4 Sep 2026: 'make it work for all the known dialects'; all three are accepted since 8 Sep 2026. Four rules bound the widening and each is load-bearing: detection is STRUCTURAL and never on `version`; all three normalise to the SAME typed columns, with the dialect carried as the metric label records_lorastats_dialect{dialect} rather than as a column; string counters are range-checked against the signed BIGINT maximum BEFORE conversion and dead-letter on overflow or a bad parse, never zeroed and never truncated; and the enumeration is CLOSED AT THREE - an unknown fourth dialect still dead-letters. rx_short_pkt, fsk_received and rx_type_arol are observed in production and are OPTIONAL because no single record carries all three. timespan is optional: the bare/string record omits it entirely.
